content: 1. Chailliet et al. (2015) conducted a cluster-randomized trial in Quebec to evaluate strategies aimed at reducing cesarean delivery rates. The study was published in the New England Journal of Medicine and demonstrated the potential impact of targeted interventions on cesarean section rates. 2. Hemminki et al. (2008) explored the unique characteristics of health services and register-based trials through a randomized trial of childbirth classes. Their findings, published in BMC Health Services Research, highlighted the role of structured education in influencing delivery outcomes. 3. Liang et al. (2004) investigated the effect of peer review and trial of labor on reducing cesarean section rates. Their study, published in the Journal of the Chinese Medical Association, emphasized the importance of collaborative review processes in improving obstetric practices. 4. Lomas et al. (1991) examined the role of opinion leaders and feedback mechanisms in implementing practice guidelines for delivery after a previous cesarean section. Their research, published in JAMA, underscored the influence of professional leadership on clinical decision-making. 5. Mohammadi et al. (2012) conducted clinical audits as a practical strategy to reduce cesarean section rates in a general hospital in Tehran, Iran. Their findings, published in the Journal of Reproductive Medicine, demonstrated the effectiveness of systematic reviews of clinical practices in achieving better outcomes. 6. Poma (1998) analyzed the impact of departmental policies on cesarean delivery rates in a community hospital setting. The study, published in Obstetrics & Gynecology, highlighted the role of institutional guidelines in shaping delivery practices. 7. Scarella et al. (2011) utilized the Ten Group Classification System in a medical audit to assess its impact on cesarean section rates. Their research, published in the European Journal of Obstetrics & Gynecology and Reproductive Biology, demonstrated the utility of this classification system in monitoring and reducing cesarean deliveries. 8. Rosenstein et al. (2015) expanded access to a collaborative 24-hour midwifery-laborist care model, which included continuous in-hospital midwifery coverage for both private and public patients. Their study, published in Obstetrics & Gynecology, showed that this model was associated with a reduction in cesarean delivery rates. 9. Keeler and Fok (1996) evaluated the effect of equalizing physician fees for vaginal and cesarean deliveries. Their study, published in Medical Care Research and Review, found that this financial intervention had minimal impact on cesarean rates. 10. Lo (2008) examined financial incentives in Taiwan, where physician fees for vaginal birth after cesarean (VBAC) and vaginal deliveries were raised to match those of cesarean sections. Despite these changes, as reported in Health Policy, financial incentives alone did not significantly alter cesarean section rates.
